The gallery

Source: vignettes/gallery.Rmd
gallery.Rmd
library(mediaplanr)
library(mediaplanr.viz)

Every chart here is drawn from one plan, so the pictures can be read against each other. It is the shape a real engagement takes: a weekly topline the whole team looks at, a TV team planning flighted buys by partner, an NBC daypart plan beneath that, and a Search team working Sunday-start weeks.

The plan 

weeks <- seq(as.Date("2026-04-06"), by = "week", length.out = 13)
shape <- c(0.6, 0.8, 1, 1.1, 1.2, 1.2, 1.1, 1, 1, 0.9, 0.8, 0.7, 0.6)
base_wk <- c(TV = 90000, Search = 45000, Social = 30000, Audio = 12000)

top_df <- expand.grid(week = weeks, channel = names(base_wk),
                      stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
top_df$planned_spend <- round(base_wk[top_df$channel] *
                                shape[match(top_df$week, weeks)])

topline <- media_plan_from_df(
  top_df, grain = "channel", time = "week",
  name = "Q2 2026 Brand Plan", advertiser = "Acme", planner = "R. Roe"
)

The TV team authors buys, not weeks, and works daily:

tv <- media_plan_from_flights(
  data.frame(
    channel = "TV", partner = c("NBC", "NBC", "ESPN", "Hulu"),
    flight_start = as.Date(c("2026-04-08", "2026-05-18", "2026-04-20", "2026-05-04")),
    flight_end   = as.Date(c("2026-05-10", "2026-06-28", "2026-06-14", "2026-06-21")),
    planned_spend = c(280000, 320000, 390000, 210000)
  ),
  grain = c("channel", "partner"), name = "TV Q2 buys",
  nickname = "TV detail", planner = "TV team", status = "to review"
)

NBC sits one level deeper again, by daypart, and Search runs on Sunday-start weeks that calendarize() bridges onto the topline’s Mondays:

nbc <- media_plan_from_df(
  data.frame(week = rep(seq(as.Date("2026-04-06"), by = "week", length.out = 12), each = 2),
             channel = "TV", partner = "NBC",
             daypart = rep(c("prime", "daytime"), 12),
             planned_spend = rep(c(38000, 12000), 12)),
  grain = c("channel", "partner", "daypart"), time = "week",
  name = "NBC upfront", status = "approved"
)

search <- media_plan_from_df(
  data.frame(week = rep(seq(as.Date("2026-04-05"), by = "week", length.out = 13), each = 2),
             channel = "Search", engine = rep(c("Google", "Bing"), 13),
             planned_spend = rep(c(41000, 6000), 13)),
  grain = c("channel", "engine"), time = "week",
  name = "Search Q2", nickname = "search", planner = "Search team"
)

plan <- revise(
  attach_subplan(attach_subplan(topline, attach_subplan(tv, nbc)), search),
  revision = 2
)
plan_tree(plan)
#> Q2 2026 Brand Plan  Rev 2                                       2,315,000
#> ├─ TV                      TV Q2 buys   flighted  3 line items  1,200,000
#> │  ├─ TV | NBC             NBC upfront  weekly    2 line items    600,000
#> │  └─ (editable)                                  2 line items    600,000
#> ├─ Search                  Search Q2    weekly    2 line items    611,000
#> └─ (editable)                                     2 line items    504,000

Structure

ec_tree() is the shape of ownership: each node a plan, each edge the cell it backs.

as_widget(ec_tree(plan), height = "320px")

tbl_tree() is the same tree a planner can sort and open. For day-to-day use it is usually the more useful of the two — the lock marker answers can I edit this here? without any geometry to read.

tbl_tree(plan)

ec_ownership() puts the question on a grid: line items down, weeks across, coloured by who owns the number. The locked block is what a scenario cannot touch.

as_widget(ec_ownership(plan), height = "300px")

Notice the left edge. Search plans Sunday-start weeks, so its spend lands partly in the week before the topline’s first Monday — calendarize() did that, and the grid shows it rather than hiding it.

Money 

as_widget(ec_sunburst(plan), height = "420px")

ec_rollup() explains one cell: the TV subplan’s partner totals stacking into the number the topline holds. This is the picture behind the error message “channel TV is planned in a subplan; edit the subplan and re-attach”.

as_widget(ec_rollup(plan, "TV"), height = "320px")

Scenarios 

s1  <- build_scenario(plan, list(target = list(channel = "Social"), scale = 1.25),
                      name = "Social +25%", nickname = "social up")
s2  <- build_scenario(s1, list(target = list(channel = "Audio"), drop = TRUE),
                      name = "Social +25%, no Audio", nickname = "no audio",
                      status = "to review")
s3  <- build_scenario(plan, list(target = list(channel = "Audio"), total = 300000),
                      name = "Audio push", nickname = "audio push")
set <- add_scenario(add_scenario(add_scenario(scenario_set(plan, "base"), s1), s2), s3)

as_widget(ec_lineage(set), height = "320px")

ec_lineage() measures each scenario against the plan it was actually derived from, so the chain reads as a chain: no audio is −144,000 against social up, not against the baseline. compare_scenarios() — and ec_compare() below — measure everything against the baseline instead. Both are true; they answer different questions.

as_widget(ec_compare(set), height = "320px")

TV and Search are flat across every scenario. That is not a coincidence in the data: they are owned by subplans, and no scenario is allowed to edit them.

The spec is data

Every chart above is a list. Printing one says what it is rather than dumping it:

spec <- ec_lineage(set)
spec
#> <mediaplanr_spec> lineage
#>   from    lineage()
#>   series  1
#>   size    2,909 bytes of JSON
#>   meta    ids, scenarios, base_name
#> 
#>   as_widget() to draw it, as_json() to send it

And it converts to JSON that any ECharts renderer accepts, with no JavaScript in it:

cat(substr(as_json(spec, pretty = TRUE), 1, 400), "...")
#> {
#>   "textStyle": {
#>     "fontFamily": "IBM Plex Sans, system-ui, -apple-system, Segoe UI, sans-serif",
#>     "color": "#18212B"
#>   },
#>   "tooltip": {
#>     "backgroundColor": "#FFFFFF",
#>     "borderColor": "#D5DBE2",
#>     "textStyle": {
#>       "color": "#18212B",
#>       "fontFamily": "IBM Plex Sans, system-ui, -apple-system, Segoe UI, sans-serif",
#>       "fontSize": 13
#>     }
#>   },
#>   "series": [
#>     {
#>       "ty ...

That is the whole reason this package emits specs rather than plots. The same list renders here, in a Shiny app, or in a frontend that has never run R — and an agent holding a tool that returns as_json(ec_lineage(set)) has given its caller a chart, not a picture of one.

Theming

The palette keeps three roles apart: an accent for the plan’s own marks, an owner ramp so one subplan is one colour in every chart, and status colours reserved for status_levels(). Pass a name or a list of overrides.

str(viz_theme("dark")[c("accent", "topline")])
#> List of 2
#>  $ accent : chr "#3FB4BE"
#>  $ topline: chr "#6F7A8A"
as_widget(ec_tree(plan, theme = list(base = "dark", accent = "#B0004F")),
          height = "320px")
